lesson.title: Software-Defined Networking: Separating the Decision from the Delivery
lesson.summary: Software-defined networking (SDN) separates the control plane, which decides where traffic should go, from the data plane, which actually forwards packets, letting a centralized controller program many switches instead of each device deciding independently.
lesson.body:
At the network layer, every router traditionally does two very different jobs inside the same box. It decides where a packet should go, running a routing protocol, exchanging information with neighboring routers, and computing a forwarding table from that information. And it also carries out that decision, physically pushing each arriving packet out the correct interface at wire speed, for every single packet, continuously. The first job is about reasoning over relatively infrequent information about topology and reachability. The second is about repeating a simple lookup an enormous number of times per second. Traditionally, both jobs live inside the same device, computed and executed locally, with each router in the network making its own independent decisions based on its own local view.

That coupling has a real cost at scale. Because every router computes its own view of the network independently, achieving a consistent, coordinated forwarding behavior across an entire network, especially a large one like a data center fabric, means relying on distributed routing protocols to converge to the same conclusion on every device, which takes time and can behave inconsistently while it is happening, particularly right after a failure. It also means any operator who wants sophisticated, network-wide traffic engineering, for example balancing load across several redundant paths in real time, has to work around each device's independent, local decision-making rather than directing the network's behavior directly.

Software-defined networking's core idea is to pull the decision-making logic, the control plane, out of individual switches entirely and move it into a centralized, or logically centralized, controller running as software, separate from the hardware doing the forwarding. The switches themselves become simpler: their job shrinks to the data plane alone, forwarding packets according to rules a controller pushes down to them, rather than computing those rules locally. A standard protocol, OpenFlow being the best known example, is one common way a controller communicates those forwarding rules down to switches, though it is not the only mechanism used in practice.

A concrete scenario shows why this matters. Imagine a data center network that wants to react instantly to a link failure by rerouting affected traffic across the fabric all at once, with full knowledge of current load on every alternative path. In a traditional network, each switch would only discover the failure and reconverge based on its own local routing protocol exchanges with its immediate neighbors, a process that takes some time to propagate and can produce transient inconsistency while different switches hold different views during convergence. With an SDN controller, the failure is reported up to the controller, which has a complete, centralized view of the entire topology and current traffic load, recomputes the affected paths in one place, and pushes new forwarding rules out to every affected switch essentially simultaneously, rather than waiting for a distributed protocol to reconverge hop by hop across the whole network.
